My multiple timelines of side quests
Carbon Neutral Club helps users understand and offset their carbon footprint through a paid membership.
What started as a conversion and clarity problem became something much bigger:
The flow revealed a better business model, and helped shift the company from individual purchase → employer-funded memberships.
I led the redesign of the core journey:
Users got a number, but not enough meaning.
The cost existed, but its logic wasn't immediately clear.
The final step asked for commitment before full confidence had been built.
Strong engagement with the calculator itself
Confusion around the final footprint number
Hesitation when entering the payment stage
More explanation could build trust, but also slow users down.
Fewer details reduced friction, but also weakened confidence.
Users needed context, but the business still needed them to complete checkout.
What should I do about it?
What am I actually paying for?
Users need context before a footprint score becomes actionable.
Add national average for comparison; have the footprint tracker move up and down based on calculator decisions.
Transparency must come before financial commitment.
Show a full breakdown of what is included and why.
Choices should feel guided, not overwhelming.
Use a progress stepper so expectations stay clear.
Users should understand what they are paying for and why.
Surface what membership includes on the choose-your-plan step.
End of 7 week project, 3 months later
This project reinforced three things for me:
Clarity builds trust more effectively than simplicity alone
Checkout is often a product strategy problem, not just a UI problem
Small experience shifts can reshape an entire business model
The most important part of this work wasn't just making the flow feel cleaner.
It was designing a system that helped users understand enough to act, and that gave the company a better way to grow.
IBM Envizi: From Reporting to Action
I was brought in to define how these products should work as one system.
Mapping the end-to-end experience across all three verticals
Identifying breakdowns in navigation, discovery, and value clarity
Running cross-functional workshops to align product, design, and leadership
Proposing a unified product direction and prioritized roadmap
This wasn't a surface-level redesign, it was about reframing the product at a system level
The product failed to connect its offerings, preventing users from discovering value beyond a single entry point.
Users didn’t understand the full product
Most users didn’t even realize the ecosystem existed.
Each vertical felt like a separate product, with mismatched navigation, layouts, and interaction patterns.
Users had to relearn the same actions across different parts of the product.
Teams moved fast, but the experience fractured.
Users came for one thing, but missed everything else.
Each vertical felt strong alone, but weak together.
A unified overview of the ecosystem, surfacing key actions, status, and entry points across all verticals.
A dedicated space to explore everything Super offers, enabling cross-vertical discovery and universal search.
A focused hub for all financial interactions, separating transactional behavior from broader product exploration.
A centralized system for incentives and engagement, connecting user actions across verticals into long-term value.
A personal control center for account, activity, and preferences, tying together the user's full relationship with the product.
If I continued the work, I'd push deeper into:
The next step would be compounding it.
IBM Envizi: From Reporting to Action
is an enterprise sustainability platform used by global organizations to track and report emissions data.
I was brought in to lead the design of a new workflow layer — one that didn't yet exist inside the product.
Defined flows across four calculation methods
Not a redesign — a new category of workflow.
No action layer inside the product
Dashboards showed emissions totals. Nothing offered a path to improve them. Seeing the problem and fixing it lived in separate worlds.
Email chains. Personal spreadsheets. No shared state. Every quarter rebuilt the same coordination system from scratch.
Users didn't know which method powered a given estimate or how to upgrade it. The data quality gap was real – and entirely unsurfaced.
No record of last quarter's outreach. No sense of who had responded. Teams repeated the same work, every cycle.
Carbon accounting demands precision. Users aren't master carbon accountants.
Four methods, branching logic. One pattern held it together.
Control without guardrails corrupts downstream reporting.
IBM Carbon was React. The product was Angular.
What users were actually struggling with inside the reporting cycle
Which problems existed across every calculation method, not just one
What opportunities were worth exploring, and which ones were distractions
Which patterns could be shared across branches to keep the system coherent
One of the first problems users faced was not knowing where to begin.
I designed a template system that converted technical sustainability goals into clear starting points.
Users start from a predefined path such as:
Not every supplier creates equal impact.
This shifted teams from broad manual outreach to focused, high-value engagement.
Choose which suppliers or products to target based on:
Without a clear outcome, supplier engagement becomes endless activity.
This gave teams a reason to act and a way to measure progress.
Instead of expecting users to invent their own process, I designed guided actions tied to each calculation method and workflow state.
Because each emissions method required different actions, this involved significant branching logic and edge-case design.
Once plans were live, users needed to know whether anything was actually improving. This transformed emissions improvement from guesswork into a visible operati

The default path: use financial spend and category factors when detailed activity data is not available.
Fills gaps with industry-average emission factors when spend or category data is the best available signal.
Combines different calculation stages and data sources in one footprint when no single method covers the whole product.
Uses supplier-reported, product-level or facility-level data when partners can submit and maintain primary evidence.
Complex systems stall when no one owns the ambiguity.
Main flows are easy. Real usability happens in exceptions.
In expert-heavy domains, users need confidence more than options.
Dashboards explain problems. Systems solve them.
Over the years, I've created, rebuilt, and maintained 8+ design systems across mobile apps, web platforms, startups, and enterprise products.
Some systems were built from scratch. Others were inherited in chaos and restructured to scale.
I treat design systems as products, not libraries.
Design systems built for products such as:
Across B2B, B2C, mobile, web, fintech, climate, travel, and enterprise.
Problems when building without a DS
Product debt hidden in plain sight
The best systems are not the biggest. They are the most adopted.
These decisions reduce hundreds of future micro-decisions.
Uses atomic design to build slot-based systems that swap elements efficiently and reduce variant complexity.
This helps teams make good decisions without asking permission constantly.
Strong systems need to scale globally.
My goal is fewer Slack questions and faster builds.
